questions.question:
A relation [latex]r(A,B)[/latex] in a relational database has 1200 tuples. The attribute [latex]A[/latex] has integer values ranging from 6 to 20, and the attribute [latex]B[/latex] has integer values ranging from 1 to 20. Assume that the attributes [latex]A[/latex] and [latex]B[/latex] are independently distributed.

The estimated number of tuples in the output of [latex]\sigma _{(A > 10)\vee(B=18)}(r)[/latex] is ____________
questions.explanation:
A takes 15 values (6-20) and B takes 20 values (1-20). The official key accepts two answers, depending on what is counted.

Method 1: estimated tuples in the output = 820
- A [latex]\gt[/latex] 10 holds for 11-20, 10 of 15 values [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]P=\frac23[/latex]
- [latex]P(B=18)=\frac1{20}[/latex]
- Independent: [latex]P(A \gt 10\vee B=18)=\frac23+\frac1{20}-\frac23\cdot\frac1{20}=\frac{41}{60}[/latex]
- Estimated tuples [latex]=1200\times\frac{41}{60}=820[/latex]

Method 2: distinct (A, B) value pairs that satisfy the condition = 205
- A [latex]\gt[/latex] 10 with any B: [latex]10\times20=200[/latex] pairs
- B = 18 with A [latex]\le[/latex] 10 (A = 6-10): 5 more pairs
- Total [latex]=200+5=205[/latex]

Answer: 820 (estimated tuples) or 205 (distinct value pairs); both are accepted

questions.question:
Let [latex]P, Q, R[/latex] and [latex]S[/latex] be the attributes of a relation in a relational schema. Let [latex]X \rightarrow Y[/latex] indicate functional dependency in the context of a relational database, where [latex]X, Y \subseteq\{P, Q, R, S\}[/latex].

Which of the following options is/are always true?

options.B: If [latex]\{P, Q\} \rightarrow\{R\}[/latex], then [latex](\{P\} \rightarrow\{R\}[/latex] or [latex]\{Q\} \rightarrow\{R\})[/latex]
options.C: If [latex](\{P\} \rightarrow\{R\}[/latex] and [latex]\{Q\} \rightarrow\{S\})[/latex], then [latex]\{P, Q\} \rightarrow\{R, S\}[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Using Armstrong's axioms (reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity) to test each claim:

- {P,Q}→{R} and {P}→{R}, does {Q}→{R} follow? No — {P}→{R} already implies {P,Q}→{R} by augmentation, so the premises give no information forcing {Q}→{R} to hold. Not always true.
- {P,Q}→{R}, does {P}→{R} or {Q}→{R} follow? No — {R} may genuinely require both P and Q together (e.g. R functionally depends on the pair but on neither attribute alone). Not always true.
- {P}→{R} and {Q}→{S}, does {P,Q}→{R,S} follow? Yes: augment {P}→{R} with Q to get {P,Q}→{R,Q}; augment {Q}→{S} with P to get {P,Q}→{P,S}; using reflexivity ({R,Q}→{R} and {P,S}→{S}) and transitivity gives {P,Q}→{R} and {P,Q}→{S}; the union rule then gives {P,Q}→{R,S}. Always true.
- {P}→{R}, does {P,Q}→{R} follow? Yes, directly by the augmentation axiom (adding Q to the left-hand side of a valid FD keeps it valid). Always true.

Answer: {P}→{R},{Q}→{S} &there4 {P,Q}→{R,S}; and {P}→{R} &there4 {P,Q}→{R}.

questions.question:
An audit of a banking transactions system has found that on an earlier occasion, two joint holders of account [latex]A [/latex] attempted simultaneous transfers of Rs. 10000 each from account [latex]A [/latex] to account [latex]B [/latex]. Both transactions read the same value, Rs. 11000, as the initial balance in [latex]A [/latex] and were allowed to go through. [latex]B [/latex] was credited Rs. 10000 twice. [latex]A [/latex] was debited only once and ended up with a balance of Rs. 1000.
Which of the following properties is/are certain to have been violated by the system?

options.B: Consistency
options.C: Isolation

questions.explanation:
This is a classic lost-update anomaly caused by two transactions reading the same stale value and overwriting each other's effects.

- Consistency is violated: the database ends up in a state that breaks the intended invariant (money should be conserved / correctly transferred), since [latex]A[/latex] should have ended up [latex]11000-20000[/latex] worth adjusted correctly but instead only one debit actually applied while both credits landed — the books don't balance as intended.
- Isolation is violated: the two concurrent transactions were not properly isolated from each other — both read [latex]A[/latex]'s balance before either had committed its update, letting their effects clash (textbook lost-update problem).
- Atomicity is not necessarily violated: each individual transaction ran to completion in full (no partial execution of a single transaction occurred).
- Durability is unrelated here: there's no indication of any committed-then-lost data due to a crash.

Answer: Consistency and Isolation

questions.question:
An ER model of a database consists of entity types A and B. These are connected by a
relationship R which does not have its own attribute. Under which one of the following
conditions, can the relational table for R be merged with that of A?

options.A: Relationship R is one-to-many and the participation of A in R is total
options.B: Relationship R is one-to-many and the participation of A in R is partial
options.C: Relationship R is many-to one and the participation of A in R is total
options.D: Relationship R is many-to one and the participation of A in R is partial

questions.explanation:
If R is many-to-one from A to B and A participates totally, each A-tuple is related to exactly one B-tuple. So B's key can be stored as a column (foreign key) in A's table without NULLs or repeats.

Answer: Relationship R is many-to-one and the participation of A in R is total

Which of the following statements are TRUE about an SQL query?
P : An SQL query can contain a HAVING clause even if it does not have a GROUP BY clause
Q : An SQL query can contain a HAVING clause only if it has a GROUP BY clause
R : All attributes used in the GROUP BY clause must appear in the SELECT clause
S : Not all attributes used in the GROUP BY clause need to appear in the SELECT clause

options.B: P and S
options.C: Q and R

questions.explanation:
The official GATE key is Q and R: HAVING used with GROUP BY, and the grouped attributes shown in SELECT.

Note: in standard SQL, HAVING without GROUP BY is allowed (the whole table is one group), and GROUP BY columns need not appear in SELECT. So P and S are also defensible.

Answer: Q and R (as per key)

questions.question: Which of the following file organizations is/are I/O efficient for the scan operation in DBMS?

options.B: Heap
options.C: Unclustered tree index

questions.explanation:
A scan reads every record of the file.

- Heap and sorted files store records packed in consecutive pages, so each page is read once [latex]\text{---}[/latex] I/O efficient.
- Unclustered tree / hash index: following the index, records are scattered in random pages; the same page may be read many times (about one I/O per record) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not efficient for a scan.

Answer: Sorted, Heap

questions.question:
A schedule of three database transactions [latex]T_1[/latex], [latex]T_2[/latex], and [latex]T_3[/latex] is shown. [latex]R_i(A)[/latex] and [latex]W_i(A)[/latex] denote read and write of data item [latex]A[/latex] by transaction [latex]T_i[/latex], [latex]i = 1, 2, 3[/latex]. The transaction [latex]T_1[/latex] aborts at the end. Which other transaction(s) will be required to be rolled back?

[latex] R_1(X) \quad W_1(Y) \quad R_2(X) \quad R_2(Y) \quad R_3(Y) \quad ABORT(T_1)[/latex]

options.B: Only [latex]T_3[/latex]
options.C: Both [latex]T_2[/latex] and [latex]T_3[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Schedule: [latex]R_1(X)\ W_1(Y)\ R_2(X)\ R_2(Y)\ R_3(Y)\ \text{ABORT}(T_1)[/latex].

[latex]T_1[/latex] writes [latex]Y[/latex] before aborting. Any transaction that subsequently read that (now-invalid) value of [latex]Y[/latex] has read "dirty" data and must be cascade-rolled-back:
- [latex]T_2[/latex] executes [latex]R_2(Y)[/latex] after [latex]W_1(Y)[/latex] — it read [latex]T_1[/latex]'s uncommitted write. [latex]T_2[/latex] must roll back.
- [latex]T_3[/latex] executes [latex]R_3(Y)[/latex] afterward too. Since no one else wrote [latex]Y[/latex] in between (only [latex]T_2[/latex] read it, without writing), [latex]T_3[/latex] also reads [latex]T_1[/latex]'s dirty value. [latex]T_3[/latex] must roll back as well.

Answer: Both T2 and T3

questions.question: In the context of relational database normalization, which of the following statements is/are true?

options.A: It is always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]3[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation
options.B: It is always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]1[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation
options.C: It is not always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition of a relation
options.D: It is not always possible to obtain a dependency-preserving [latex]2[/latex]NF decomposition of a relation

questions.explanation:
Standard relational-normalization theory results:

- 3NF: It is a classical theorem that every relation schema has a dependency-preserving (and lossless-join) decomposition into 3NF, via the synthesis algorithm on a minimal cover of the FDs. True.
- 1NF: 1NF only requires atomic domains; a relation can always trivially satisfy/preserve 1NF without needing to give up any functional dependency (no decomposition is even forced). True.
- BCNF: It is a well-known counterexample-backed result that a dependency-preserving BCNF decomposition is not always possible — achieving BCNF can force us to lose some functional dependency (they can only be checked by joining relations back together, which is expensive/impossible to enforce locally). True (i.e., "not always possible" is a true statement).
- 2NF: Since a dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition always exists, and 3NF automatically implies 2NF, a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition is always achievable too. So "it is not always possible to get a dependency-preserving 2NF decomposition" is false.

Answer: Dependency-preserving decompositions always exist for 3NF and for 1NF; it is not always possible for BCNF.

Y[latex]\rightarrow[/latex] VX
Y [latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Z
Which of the following is irreducible equivalent for this set of functional dependencies ?

Y [latex]\rightarrow[/latex]Z

questions.question:
Consider two relations describing teams and players in a sports league:

[latex]teams(tid, tname):tid, tname [/latex] are team-id and team-name, respectively
[latex]players(pid, pname, tid):pid,pname,tid[/latex] denote player-id, player-name and the team-id of the player, respectively

Which ONE of the following tuple relational calculus queries returns the name of the players who play for the team having name as 'MI'?

options.A: [latex] \{ p.pname \mid p \in players \wedge \exists t ( t \in teams \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge t.tname = 'MI' ) \} [/latex]
options.B: [latex] \{ p.pname \mid p \in teams \wedge \exists t ( t \in players \wedge p.tid = t.tid \wedge t.tname = 'MI' ) \} [/latex]
options.C: [latex] \{ p.pname \mid p \in players \wedge \exists t ( t \in teams \wedge t.tname = 'MI' ) \} [/latex]
options.D: [latex] \{ p.pname \mid p \in teams \wedge \exists t ( t \in players \wedge t.tname = 'MI' ) \} [/latex]

questions.explanation:
We want, for each player [latex]p[/latex] in [latex]\text{players}[/latex], their name, restricted to only those players whose [latex]tid[/latex] matches some team [latex]t[/latex] in [latex]\text{teams}[/latex] with [latex]t.tname=\text{'MI'}[/latex].

This is exactly:
[latex]\{p.pname\mid p\in players\ \wedge\ \exists t(t\in teams\ \wedge\ p.tid=t.tid\ \wedge\ t.tname=\text{'MI'})\}[/latex]

The key correctness checks: the outer variable [latex]p[/latex] must range over [latex]players[/latex] (not [latex]teams[/latex], since we want player names), and the join condition [latex]p.tid=t.tid[/latex] must actually be present inside the existential (options that drop this join condition would incorrectly return every player's name whenever team 'MI' exists at all, regardless of which team the player is actually on).

Answer: {p.pname | p∈players ∧ ∃t(t∈teams ∧ p.tid=t.tid ∧ t.tname='MI')}

questions.question:
Consider a relational table r with sufficient number of records, having attributes [latex]A_{1}, A_{2},..., A_{n}[/latex] and let [latex]1\leq p\leq n[/latex] . Two queries Q1 and Q2 are given below.

[latex]Q1:\pi _{A_{1}....A_{n}}(\sigma _{A_{p}=c}(r)) [/latex] where c is a constant
[latex]Q2:\pi _{A1....A_{n}}(\sigma _{c_{1}\leq A_{p}\leq c_{2}}(r)) [/latex] where [latex]c_{1}[/latex] and [latex]c_{2}[/latex] are constants

The database can be configured to do ordered indexing on [latex]A_{p}[/latex] or hashing on [latex]A_{p}[/latex].

Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.A: Ordered indexing will always outperform hashing for both queries
options.B: Hashing will always outperform ordered indexing for both queries
options.C: Hashing will outperform ordered indexing on Q1, but not on Q2
options.D: Hashing will outperform ordered indexing on Q2, but not on Q1.

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Q1 is an equality search: a hash index finds it in about one access, faster than walking a tree.
- Q2 is a range search: hashing scatters values, so it cannot do ranges. An ordered index can.

Answer: Hashing will outperform ordered indexing on Q1, but not on Q2

questions.question:
Consider the relation [latex]R(P,Q,S,T,X,Y,Z,W)[/latex] with the following functional dependencies.

[latex]PQ\rightarrow X;\quad P\rightarrow YX;\quad Q\rightarrow Y; \quad Y\rightarrow ZW[/latex]

Consider the decomposition of the relation R into the constituent relations according to the following two decomposition schemes.

[latex]D1:\quad R=[(P,QS,T);\;(P,T,X);\;(Q,Y);\;(Y,Z,W)][/latex]
[latex]D2:\quad R=[(P,Q,S);\;(T,X);\;(Q,Y);\;(Y,Z,W)][/latex]

Which one of the following options is correct?

options.A: D1 is a lossless decomposition, but D2 is a lossy decomposition.
options.B: D1 is a lossy decomposition, but D2 is a lossless decomposition.
options.C: Both D1 and D2 are lossless decompositions.
options.D: Both D1 and D2 are lossy decompositions.

questions.explanation:
D1: join step by step on common attributes that are keys of one side:
- (P, Q, S, T) with (P, T, X) on PT: [latex]P\rightarrow X[/latex] so PT [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] X True
- with (Q, Y) on Q: [latex]Q\rightarrow Y[/latex] True
- with (Y, Z, W) on Y: [latex]Y\rightarrow ZW[/latex] True
So D1 is lossless.

D2: (T, X) shares no attribute with the other relations, so joining it gives a cross product [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] lossy.

Answer: D1 is lossless, but D2 is lossy

questions.question:
Consider the following two phase locking protocol. Suppose a transaction T accesses (for read or write operations), a certain set of objects {O1,... ,Ok}. This is done in the following manner:
Step 1. T acquires exclusive locks to O1,...,Ok in increasing order of their addresses.
Step 2. The required operations are performed.
Step 3. All locks are released.
This protocol will

options.B: guarantee neither serializability nor deadlock-freedom
options.C: guarantee serializability but not deadlock-freedom

All locks are taken before any operation and released only at the end [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] a two-phase locking schedule [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] serializable.

questions.question:
Consider the following relational schema:

Suppliers(sid:integer, sname:string, city:string, street:string)
Parts(pid:integer, pname:string, color:string)
Catalog(sid:integer, pid:integer, cost:real)
Assume that, in the suppliers relation above, each supplier and each street within a city has a unique name, and (sname, city) forms a candidate key. No other functional dependencies are implied other than those implied by primary and candidate keys. Which one of the following is TRUE about the above schema?

options.B: The schema is in 3NF but not in BCNF
options.C: The schema is in 2NF but not in 3NF

questions.question:
Let the set of functional dependencies [latex]F=\{QR\rightarrow S,R\rightarrow P,S\rightarrow Q\}[/latex] hold on a relation schema X = (PQRS). X is not in BCNF. Suppose X is decomposed into two schemas Y and Z where Y = (PR) and Z = (QRS).
Consider the two statements given below:

I. Both Y and Z are in BCNF
II. Decomposition of X into Y and Z is dependency preserving and lossless.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?

options.B: I only
options.C: II only

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Y(P, R): R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P with R as key [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] BCNF.
- Z(Q, R, S): QR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S and S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q. Keys are QR and RS. In S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q, S is not a superkey [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Z is not BCNF. So I is false.
- Dependencies: R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is in Y; QR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S and S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q are in Z [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] preserved.
- Lossless: common attribute R, and R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P makes R a key of Y [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] lossless. So II is true.

Answer: II only

questions.question:
Consider the following table named Student in a relational database. The primary key of this table is rollNum.
[latex]\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \\ rollNum&name&gender&marks \\ \hline 1&Naman&M&62\\ \hline 2&Aliya&F&70 \\ \hline 3&Aliya &F&80 \\ \hline 4&James&M&82\\ \hline 5&Swati&F&65\\ \hline \end{array} [/latex]
The SQL query below is executed on this database.

SELECT *
FROM Student
WHERE gender = 'F' AND
 marks > 65;

The number of rows returned by the query is ______
questions.explanation:
Rows with gender = 'F' and marks [latex]\gt[/latex] 65:
- Aliya, 70 True
- Aliya, 80 True
- Swati, 65 False (65 is not greater than 65)

SELECT * returns full rows, so the duplicate name does not matter.

Answer: 2

questions.question:
Consider a simple checkpointing protocol and the following set of operations in the log.
(start, T4); (write, T4, y, 2, 3); (start, T1); (commit, T4); (write, T1, z, 5, 7);
(checkpoint);
(start, T2); (write, T2, x, 1, 9); (commit, T2); (start, T3), (write, T3, z, 7, 2);
If a crash happens now and the system tries to recover using both undo and redo operations, what are the contents of the undo list and the redo list?

options.B: Undo: T3, T1; Redo: T2, T4
options.C: Undo: none; Redo: T2, T4, T3, T1
options.D: Undo: T3, T1, T4; Redo: T2

questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- T4 committed before the checkpoint [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] already safe, nothing to do.
- T1 started before the checkpoint and never committed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] undo.
- T2 committed after the checkpoint [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] redo.
- T3 never committed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] undo.

Answer: Undo: T3, T1; Redo: T2
